newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS - Coffee vols surge as players turn to put.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Coffee vols surge as players turn to put.

text.p: Volatilities perked up on coffee puts Thursday as options players sought bigger premiums for protection against a sharp U-turn from racing futures.
Cocoa options were almost completely abandoned in London, as the focus remained on the dire chart prospects surrounding the futures and sterling's movements against the French franc.
In coffee, Thursday's session saw a total 550 lots of May $1,650, $1,550 and $1,450 puts traded with vols spiking higher to about 43-45 percent from 37-38 percent last week.

"We (futures) were due about $50-75 higher today... it looks like the volatility should be higher than what it has been in the last weeks. Anything below 40 percent wasn't really realistic," said one options market maker.
Robusta futures, pursuing a relentless surge in New York-listed Arabicas, broke above $1,700 a tonne for the first time in six months and technically looked fit to reach $1,740.

Gains have totalled 43 percent since early January, and although a correction was overdue, few players were prepared to sell into a rallying market. "Who's going to jump in front of a runaway train," commented one trader.
Sentiment reached boiling point this week as a major strike in Colombia looked set to cripple exports just as signs emerged for a lower-than-expected Brazilian crop in 1997/98.
But some traders remained on guard for an ambush by hedge funds.
"People are taking protection against a sharp drop in futures," said one. Sellers of puts, on the other hand, were possibly volatility traders trying to lock in the premium.
March option vols were flat at 38 percent, but they too should make a foray to 41 percent before Wednesday's expiry, traders said.
Some March and May in-the-money calls were juggled this week. Traders said these could either be part of a strategy to sell futures, or simply trade liquidation of shorts.
March was heading for a smooth expiry on Wednesday, with much of the open interest left behind the current price level.
Cocoa saw hardly any trade this week, except some March 950 and 1,050 stg calls on Thursday but some market makers continued to advocate buying out-the-money calls basis May and July.

"We feel that the futures market has reached a level where it's absorbed a lot of origin selling and the funds have gone short of it," said one. "The market is basically setting itself up for a very strong short covering rally."
Recommended strikes were July 950 stg and May 925 currently worth 20 stg with vols around 20-19 percent.
But sterling's firmness against the French franc, the currency in which Ivorians sell cocoa, deterred buyers.
"People believe what's the point of buying upside or downside risk because at the moment the market is being sapped of its strength because of the currency," said one.
Futures recorded some gains on Thursday after tumbling to new lows Wednesday, and the May contract looked set to close above the 870 level which could be technically encouraging.
The biggest cliffhanger is Ivorian arrivals, which have so far shown no signs of tailing off with the total main crop almost approaching last year's record level.
Trading in white sugar options was quiet as usual although interest was noted in the May white/raw sugar differential and also to buy May and August out-of-the-money calls.
Traders said strike prices on the further forward months tended to hover around $290 but general options activity was subdued with narrowing volatilities.
